title: 7 Reasons Your Students Dislike You
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin lists seven behaviors that can cause students to dislike a teacher, framing likability as central to effective classroom management because it drives rapport and gives consequences real weight. The reasons include inconsistency, which breeds resentment and distrust; disorganization, which undermines respect and authority; unclear expectations, which frustrate and destabilize students; excessive talking, which causes students to tune out; over-helping, which suffocates independence; being boring, which invites disengagement; and being chronically grumpy, which poisons interactions especially around misbehavior. He closes by framing likability as an earned, buildable trait rather than a fixed personality trait, achievable through honest self-assessment and targeted change.
points: Frames likability as foundational to classroom management because it drives rapport and makes consequences meaningful to students.
Cites inconsistency and disorganization as major likability killers, since both erode students' trust and respect.
Warns that unclear expectations and excessive talking frustrate students and cause tune-out and misbehavior.
Identifies over-helping ('suffocating') as underrated but damaging, since it removes independence and breeds resentment.
Positions being boring or chronically grumpy as final likability barriers, both of which are avoidable through self-awareness and effort.
quotes: When you’re inconsistent, students believe—and rightly so—that your classroom management plan isn’t applied fairly and equally to everyone.

Respect is closely linked to likability. If your room is cluttered and you have papers strewn atop your desk, if you appear rushed and underprepared, then your students won’t view you as a leader worth following.
Not knowing what is expected for any length of time during the school day is massively frustrating for students.
They kneel down, hot-breath close and usher in learned helplessness.
Well-liked teachers are constantly assessing how their students are responding to instruction.
Lecturing, scolding, questioning, and other acts of intimidation don’t work in this day and age. They only sabotage your own peace and enjoyment and bring about more misbehavior, not less.
